summary: Specifies a negotiation mechanism for GSS-API so peers can choose a common security mechanism. If the chosen mechanism supports per-message integrity, the negotiation itself is protected against an attacker. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: GSS-API is an interface that lets the same application use different security mechanisms, such as Kerberos. Before anything else can happen, the two sides have to agree which mechanism to use. This RFC defines that agreement, and a check that detects an attacker tampering with the list of offered mechanisms.

questions: what is the gss-api negotiation mechanism
subtitle: How two programs using GSS-API agree on a shared security mechanism, and notice if an attacker tampers with the choice.

tldr.problem: GSS-API lets two peers use whichever security mechanism they both have credentials for, but it does not say how the peers find out whether they have one in common.
tldr.mechanism: SPNEGO is a pseudo mechanism that carries a list of mechanisms in preference order, has the responder pick one and say so, and, where the chosen mechanism can protect messages, exchanges integrity codes over the list so an alteration is detected.
tldr.outcome: Peers end up with a common mechanism, and when an attacker could have pushed them to a weaker choice, the negotiation fails or falls back rather than silently accepting it. The document obsoletes RFC 2478 and is not compatible with implementations of that older version.

facts.label: MIC input
facts.value: GSS_GetMIC() over the DER encoding of the MechTypeList value

today: RFC 4178 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It obsoleted RFC 2478 and has not been obsoleted since. It defines how GSS-API peers agree on a common security mechanism, and the integrity check that stops an attacker altering that choice.

sections.title: The Negotiation Problem
sections.content:
The GSS-API, RFC 2743, provides a generic interface that can be layered on top of different security mechanisms, so that if communicating peers acquire GSS-API credentials for the same security mechanism, a security context may be established between them, subject to policy. GSS-API does not, however, prescribe the method by which peers establish whether they have a common security mechanism.

The Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation (SPNEGO) mechanism is a pseudo security mechanism that enables GSS-API peers to determine in band whether their credentials support a common set of one or more GSS-API security mechanisms; if so, it invokes the normal security context establishment for a selected common mechanism. It is most useful for applications that depend on GSS-API implementations and share multiple mechanisms between the peers.

The model is that the initiator proposes a list of security mechanisms in decreasing preference order, and the acceptor, also known as the target, either accepts the initiator's preferred mechanism, which is the first in the list, or chooses one of the available mechanisms from the offered list; if neither is acceptable, the acceptor rejects the proposed values. The target then informs the initiator of its choice. Once a common mechanism is chosen, mechanism-specific options may be negotiated as part of the selected mechanism's context establishment, but those negotiations are internal to the mechanism and opaque to SPNEGO.

If per-message integrity services are available on the established mechanism context, the negotiation is protected to make sure the mechanism list has not been modified. In cases where an attacker could have materially influenced the negotiation, peers exchange message integrity code (MIC) tokens to confirm that the mechanism list has not been modified. If no action of an attacker could have materially modified the outcome, the exchange of MIC tokens is optional, which gives interoperability with existing implementations while still protecting the negotiation, at the cost of increased complexity.

The negotiation data is encapsulated in context-level tokens, so callers of the GSS-API need not be aware of the existence of the negotiation tokens, only of the new pseudo security mechanism. A failure in the negotiation phase causes a major status code to be returned, GSS_S_BAD_MECH.
sections.plainLanguage: One side lists the security mechanisms it can use, best first. The other side picks one and says so. The rest of the exchange then uses that one mechanism, as if SPNEGO were not there.

sections.title: The Negotiation Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure assumes that per-message integrity services are available on the established mechanism context. The GSS-API initiator invokes GSS_Init_sec_context() as normal but requests that SPNEGO be used, either explicitly or as the default mechanism. The implementation then generates a negotiation token containing a list of one or more security mechanisms that are available from the credentials used for this context establishment, and optionally the initial mechanism token for the first mechanism in the list. That list MUST NOT contain the SPNEGO mechanism itself or any mechanism for which the client does not have appropriate credentials.

The initiator application sends the token to the target application, which passes it to GSS_Accept_sec_context(). The acceptor then does one of four things. If none of the proposed mechanisms are acceptable, the negotiation is terminated, GSS_Accept_sec_context() indicates GSS_S_BAD_MECH, and the acceptor may output a negotiation token containing a reject state. If the initiator's preferred mechanism is not accepted, or it is accepted but is not the acceptor's most preferred mechanism, GSS_Accept_sec_context() indicates GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED and the acceptor MUST output a negotiation token containing a request-mic state. If at least one additional negotiation token from the initiator is needed, the acceptor indicates GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED and outputs a token containing an accept-incomplete state. Otherwise, no further token is needed, it indicates GSS_S_COMPLETE and outputs a token containing an accept-complete state.

Unless the preference order is specified by the application, the policy by which the target chooses a mechanism is an implementation-specific local matter. In the absence of an application-specified preference order or other policy, the target SHALL choose the first mechanism in the initiator's proposed list for which it has valid credentials.

The target application returns the negotiation token to the initiator application, which passes it to GSS_Init_sec_context(). Context initialization then continues by the normal GSS-API conventions for the selected mechanism, with the tokens of that mechanism encapsulated in negotiation messages, until GSS_S_COMPLETE is returned for both sides by the selected security mechanism. MIC tokens are then skipped or exchanged according to Section 5.

Two details matter in practice. To avoid conflicts with the use of MIC tokens by SPNEGO, partially established contexts MUST NOT be used for per-message calls, so prot_ready_state MUST be set to false on return from GSS_Init_sec_context() and GSS_Accept_sec_context(), even if the underlying mechanism returned true. And to avoid an extra round trip, the first context establishment token of the initiator's preferred mechanism SHOULD be embedded in the initial negotiation message; this is called the optimistic mechanism token, and using it lets the initiator recover from non-fatal errors before a mechanism has been chosen. Where generating that token is expensive, implementations MAY omit it.
sections.plainLanguage: The initiator sends its list, the responder answers with one of four verdicts, and the two sides then run the chosen mechanism to the end. Each verdict says something different: no common mechanism, a mechanism chosen but more messages needed, a mechanism chosen and ready, or a request to prove the list was not tampered with.

sections.title: The Negotiation Tokens
sections.content:
The type definitions assume an ASN.1 module with the object identifier iso.org.dod.internet.security.mechanism.snego.modules.spec2, with explicit and non-automatic tagging. The encoding of the SPNEGO protocol messages must obey the Distinguished Encoding Rules of ASN.1, as described in ITU-T Recommendation X.690.

Each OID in the model represents one GSS-API mechanism, or one variant of it. MechType is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER and MechTypeList is a SEQUENCE OF MechType. The syntax of the initial negotiation token follows the initialContextToken syntax defined in Section 3.1 of RFC 2743, and the SPNEGO pseudo mechanism is identified by the object identifier 1.3.6.1.5.5.2. Subsequent tokens MUST NOT be encapsulated in that GSS-API generic token framing.

NegotiationToken is a choice between negTokenInit and negTokenResp. The initial token carries four optional fields after the mechanism list: mechTypes, the one or more security mechanisms available for the initiator in decreasing preference order; reqFlags, the service options requested to establish the context, inherited from RFC 2478 and not integrity protected, which the initiator SHOULD omit and the acceptor MUST ignore; mechToken, the optimistic mechanism token; and mechListMIC, an MIC token for the mechanism list.

The response token carries negState, an enumerated value that is accept-completed, accept-incomplete, reject or request-mic and is REQUIRED in the first reply from the target and OPTIONAL thereafter, with the state to be inferred from the state of the negotiated mechanism context when it is absent; supportedMech, which is present only in the first reply from the target and MUST be one of the mechanisms offered by the initiator; responseToken, holding tokens specific to the selected mechanism; and mechListMIC.
sections.plainLanguage: The first message carries the list of mechanisms and, if available, a first token for the favourite one. The reply carries a state, the mechanism that was chosen, and any token for that mechanism. Everything is encoded with the strict ASN.1 encoding rules.

sections.title: Protecting the Mechanism List
sections.content:
If the mechanism selected by the negotiation does not support integrity protection, no mechListMIC token is used. Otherwise, if the accepted mechanism is the most preferred mechanism of both the initiator and the acceptor, the MIC token exchange is OPTIONAL. A mechanism is the acceptor's most preferred mechanism if there is no other mechanism that the acceptor would have preferred over the accepted mechanism had it been present in the mechanism list.

In all other cases, MIC tokens MUST be exchanged after the mechanism context is fully established. The MIC token is computed over the mechanism list in the initial negotiation message by invoking GSS_GetMIC(), with the input context_handle being the established mechanism context, the input qop_req being 0, and the input message being the DER encoding of the value of type MechTypeList contained in the mechTypes field. The input message is NOT the DER encoding of the type '[0] MechTypeList'.

Who sends first depends on which side sends the last mechanism token. If the selected mechanism exchanges an even number of mechanism tokens, so the acceptor sends the last one, then the acceptor either indicates GSS_S_COMPLETE without a mechListMIC token when the exchange is optional, or indicates GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED with a mechListMIC token and an accept-incomplete state. When the exchange is required, the acceptor indicates GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED and includes a mechListMIC token. The initiator then either verifies a correct token and completes, terminates the negotiation with GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN if an included token is incorrect, completes with no output token when no token was included and none was required, or terminates with GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN when no token was included but one was required.

If the chosen mechanism exchanges an odd number of mechanism tokens, so the initiator sends the last one, then a mechListMIC token MUST be included if the negState was request-mic in the first reply; otherwise it is OPTIONAL. If the optimistic mechanism token is the only mechanism token for the initiator's preferred mechanism, the token is OPTIONAL either way, and GSS_Init_sec_context() indicates GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED regardless. There is one special case: if the optimistic mechanism token is also the last mechanism token, and the target sent a request-mic state but the initiator did not send a mechListMIC token, then the target MUST include a mechListMIC token in that first reply, and the initiator MUST verify it and send one back for the target to verify.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the secure channel is up, each side signs the list of mechanisms that was offered. If the two sides would both have preferred the same mechanism, the check is optional; otherwise it is required, and a bad or missing signature ends the negotiation.

sections.title: Extending the Protocol
sections.content:
Two mechanisms are provided for extensibility. First, the ASN.1 structures in this specification may be expanded by IETF standards action, and implementations receiving unknown fields MUST ignore those fields.

Second, object identifiers corresponding to a desired mechanism attribute, that is, mechanism variants, may be included in the set of preferred mechanisms by an initiator. The acceptor can honour this request by preferring mechanisms that have the included attributes. Future work within the Kitten working group was expected to standardize common attributes that SPNEGO mechanisms may wish to support; for now it is enough to say that initiators MAY include object identifiers that do not correspond to mechanisms, and that such identifiers MAY influence the acceptor's choice of mechanism.

Because a mechanism that the acceptor would have preferred might be in the initiator's list, the acceptor MUST demand the MIC token exchange in that case. As a consequence, acceptors MUST demand the MIC token exchange if they support negotiation of attributes not available in the initiator's preferred mechanism, regardless of whether the initiator actually requested those attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol can grow new fields, and a peer can hint at properties it would like in a mechanism. The catch is that any such hint makes the integrity check mandatory, because it changes what the two sides would have chosen.

sections.title: What the Protection Guarantees
sections.content:
To produce the MIC token for the mechanism list, the mechanism must provide integrity protection. When the selected mechanism does not support integrity protection, the negotiation is vulnerable: an active attacker can force it to use a security mechanism that is not mutually preferred but is acceptable to the target.

When per-message integrity services are available on the established mechanism context, and the mechanism list was altered by an adversary so that a mechanism that is not mutually preferred could be selected, the protocol gives two guarantees. If the last mechanism token is sent by the initiator, both peers fail. If the last mechanism token is sent by the acceptor, the acceptor does not complete, and the initiator, at worst, completes with its preferred mechanism selected. The negotiation may not be terminated if an alteration was made but had no material impact.

The protection of the negotiation depends on the strength of the integrity protection, so the strength of SPNEGO is no stronger than the integrity protection of the weakest mechanism acceptable to GSS-API peers. Where several mechanisms have similar context tokens but different semantics, so that one mechanism's tokens might pass for another's, there may be downgrade or similar attacks; for example, if a family of mechanisms uses the same context token syntax for two or more variants and depends on the object identifier in the initial token's wrapper but does not protect that object identifier, there may be an attack against those mechanisms, and SPNEGO does not generally defeat such attacks. In all cases the communicating peers are exposed to the denial of service threat.
sections.plainLanguage: The check is only as strong as the weakest mechanism both sides accept, and it does not protect against mechanisms that look alike to an attacker. In every case an attacker can at least stop the negotiation from finishing.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2478
sections.content:
SPNEGO implementations in Microsoft Windows 2000, Windows XP and Windows Server 2003 behave as follows: no mechListMIC is produced, and mechListMIC is not processed if one is provided; if the initiator sends the last mechanism token, the acceptor sends back a negotiation token with an accept-complete state and no mechListMIC token. In addition, an incorrect object identifier, 1.2.840.48018.1.2.2, can be used to identify the GSS-API Kerberos Version 5 mechanism.

The RFC lists the changes made to be compatible with those legacy implementations: NegTokenTarg is changed to negTokenResp and is the message format for all subsequent negotiation tokens; NegTokenInit is the message for the initial negotiation message, and only that message; mechTypes in negTokenInit is not optional; and if the selected mechanism is also the most preferred mechanism for both peers, it is safe to omit the MIC tokens. If at least one of the two peers implements the updated pseudo mechanism, the negotiation is protected.

The changes made to address problems in RFC 2478 are that reqFlags is not protected and therefore should not affect the negotiation, DER encoding is required, the GSS_GetMIC() input is clarified, per-message integrity services are requested for the negotiated mechanism, and two MIC tokens are exchanged, one in each direction. The RFC notes that an implementation conforming to it will not interoperate with a strict RFC 2478 implementation, even if it always sends a mechListMIC token.
sections.plainLanguage: The older version of this protocol shipped in Windows systems that never checked the mechanism list. This version is written to work with those systems while still protecting the negotiation whenever either side is updated.

viz.caption: Illustrative, not from the RFC: the negotiation exchange

messages.label: NEGOTOKENINIT
messages.note: The mechanism list in preference order, plus the optimistic mechanism token.

messages.label: CHOOSE
messages.note: The target picks the first mechanism it has credentials for, unless its own policy says otherwise.

messages.label: NEGOTOKENRESP
messages.note: The chosen mechanism and a state: accept-completed, accept-incomplete, reject or request-mic.

messages.label: MIC TOKEN
messages.note: An integrity code over the mechanism list, exchanged when the choice was not mutually preferred.

viz.caption: The four states the target can return

items.label: accept-completed
items.desc: No further negotiation message is expected and the security context is established.

items.label: accept-incomplete
items.desc: At least one more negotiation message is needed to establish the context.

items.label: request-mic
items.desc: The exchange of MIC tokens is REQUIRED if per-message integrity is available. Only in the first reply.

viz.caption: What the two token types carry

items.title: mechTypes
items.text: The mechanisms the initiator offers, most preferred first. It may not list SPNEGO itself or any mechanism it lacks credentials for.

items.title: reqFlags
items.text: Requested service options, inherited from RFC 2478. It is not integrity protected, so the initiator should omit it and the acceptor must ignore it.

items.title: mechToken
items.text: The optimistic mechanism token: the first token of the initiator's preferred mechanism, sent early to save a round trip.

items.title: supportedMech
items.text: The mechanism the target chose. It must be one the initiator offered, and appears only in the first reply.

items.title: responseToken
items.text: Tokens belonging to the selected mechanism.

items.title: mechListMIC
items.text: An integrity code over the mechanism list, computed with GSS_GetMIC() over the DER encoding of the MechTypeList value.
